## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.98654.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.98654.3.sa3)

This work brings a computational approach to the study of promoters and transcription. The paper is improved but there are still factual errors and implausible explanations. I am not convinced by the response from the authors, concerning the promoter -35 element, in their rebuttal.

Comments on author rebuttal:

- We respectfully but strongly disagree that our analysis has misrepresented the true nature of -35 boxes. First, accounting for more A's at position 5 in the PWM is not going to lead to a "critical error." This is because positions 4-6 of the motif barely have any information content (bits) compared to positions 1-3 (see Fig 1A).

The analysis does misrepresent the consensus -35 element, which is, unequivocally, TTGACA. I agree that positions 4-6 of the element are less well-conserved.

- This assertion is not just based on our own PWM, but based on ample precedent in the literature. In PMID 14529615, TTG is present in 38% of all -35 boxes, but ACA only in 8%.

This does not mean that TTGACA is not the consensus, or that "ACA" is not important at promoters where it's present.

- In PMID 29388765, with the -10 instance TATAAT, the -35 instance TTGCAA yields stronger promoters compared to the -35 instance TTGACA (See their Figure 3B).

This is a known phenomenon and results from "perfect" promoters being limited at the point of RNA polymerase promoter escape (because the RNAP struggles to "let go" of perfect promoters). This does not mean the TTGACA is not the consensus. Indeed, and this is a key point, it is evident in the figure the authors refer to that TTGACA stimulates more transcription than alternative -35 sequences when -10 elements are not perfect.

- In PMID 29745856 (Figure 2), the most information content lies in positions 1-3, with the A and C at position 5 both nearly equally represented, as in our PWM.

The motif shown in this paper suffers from exactly the same issue as the paper under review; the variable spacing between the -35 hexamer and -10 element isn't taken into account by MEME.

- In PMID 33958766 (Figure 1) an experimentally-derived -35 box is even reduced to a "partial" -35 box which only includes positions 1 and 2, with consensus: TTnnnn.

This paper does not show an "experimentally-derived -35 box" in Figure 1 (or anywhere else, as far as I can see).

- In addition, we did not derive the PWMs as the reviewer describes. The PWMs we use are based on computational predictions that are in excellent agreement with experimental results. Specifically, the PWMs we use are from PMID 29728462, which acquired 145 -10 and -35 box sequences from the top 3.3% of computationally predicted boxes from Regulon DB.

The paper mentioned states "for the genomic RNAP logo, sequences were taken from computationally predicted RNAP binding sites on RegulonDB" so these are not experimentally defined promoters? It's not obvious from the paper, or regulon DB, which sequences these are or how they were predicted.

- Thank you for pointing out that our original submission was incomplete in this regard. We address these concerns by new analyses, including some new experiments. First, Rho dependent termination is associated with the RUT motif, which is very rich in Cytosines (PMID: 30845912). Given that our sequences confer between 65%-78% of AT-content, canonical rho dependent termination is unlikely. However, we computationally searched for rho-dependent terminators using the available code from PMID: 30845912, but the algorithm did not identify any putative RUTs. Because this analysis was not informative, we did not include it in the paper.

I don't believe it is the case that Rho absolutely requires a RUT sequence. My understanding is that, if an RNA is not translated, Rho will intervene (e.g. see PMID: 18487194).

- We respectfully disagree that the reviewer's point is pertinent because what the reviewer is referring to is the likelihood that the sequence is a promoter, which indeed increases with AT content, but we are focused on the likelihood that a sequence becomes a promoter through DNA mutation

I disagree that this distinction is relevant. An AT-rich sequence will much more closely resemble a promoter by chance than a GC rich sequence. As an extreme example, the sequence TTTTTT can be converted into a reasonable -10 element by one change (to TATTTT) but the sequence GGGGGG can't.

results.result: The authors constructed a mutagenesis library from 25 promoter island templates (~1 kbps regions enriched with -10 and -35 boxes), generating 245,639 unique daughter sequences with ~2.5 point mutations per daughter and 93% coverage of possible single mutational neighbors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 describe the library construction with appropriate experimental detail. The coverage metric (C5) and library size (C4) are well-documented with supporting figures. The characterization of parent sequences (C2, C3) uses established PWM methods and is supported by supplementary data.

results.result: Among the 50 parent sequences (25 templates, both strands), 10 sequences exhibited promoter activity before mutagenesis: 3 on the top strand, 7 on the bottom strand, with 2 bidirectional promoters, while 40 sequences were non-promoters with average fluorescence of 1.39 a.u.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C10 characterize the baseline promoter activity using the sort-seq fluorescence assay. The 1.5 a.u. threshold is justified by the sigmoid curve inflection point (C15). The classification is supported by experimental measurements and appropriate controls shown in supplementary figures.

results.result: The TGn motif (extended -10 box) is present upstream of -10 boxes in 30% of parent sequences, but only 20% of these sequences with the TGn motif exhibit promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 demonstrate that the TGn motif alone is insufficient for promoter activity. The computational motif analysis is straightforward and the percentages are clearly stated. This finding challenges the assumption that extended -10 boxes reliably predict promoter function.

results.result: The probability of promoter emergence (Pnew) varies 205-fold among non-promoter parents (0.002 to 0.41, median 0.046) and does not correlate with the number of -10 or -35 boxes, GC-content, or daughter sequence count. Six k-mers showed correlation with Pnew but were driven by a single outlier.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C21 and C121-C122 demonstrate that simple sequence features do not predict promoter emergence. The statistical analyses (linear regression, p-values) are appropriate, and the authors correctly identify that k-mer correlations are artifacts of an outlier (P8-RFP). The sigmoid relationship between parent fluorescence and Pnew (C15) is well-supported.

results.result: Mutual information analysis identified 68 hotspots (34 in promoters, 34 in non-promoters) where mutations significantly affect fluorescence. Hotspots overlap significantly more with -10 and -35 boxes in biological sequences than scrambled controls, but only ~13% of all -10 and -35 boxes in parents contribute to promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C38 use mutual information to identify functionally important regions. The chi-squared tests (C28, C34, C35) appropriately compare biological vs. scrambled sequences. The key finding (C38) that only ~13% of motifs are functional is well-supported and challenges the assumption that all predicted motifs are active. The 90th percentile threshold for hotspot identification is reasonable.

results.result: Mutations created 1,562 new -10 boxes and 1,576 new -35 boxes across all daughter sequences, with ~22% appropriately spaced from cognate boxes and ~7.3% of -10 boxes including the TGn motif. However, only 9 of these new boxes (~0.3%) significantly increased fluorescence by >0.5 a.u., indicating that creating new promoter motifs rarely results in de novo promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 and C123-C124 demonstrate the central finding that new motif creation is insufficient for promoter emergence. The Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction are appropriate for multiple testing. The 0.5 a.u. threshold is reasonable for biological significance. This is a major finding challenging the sufficiency of motif presence for function.

results.result: Two specific examples demonstrate de novo promoter emergence: P16-RFP gains activity when a -10 box is created 17 bp downstream of a -35 box (TAAACA→TAAACt, +1.99 a.u., 11.2-fold increase), and P1-RFP gains activity when a -35 box is created 18 bp upstream of a -10 box (ATGAGT→tTGAGT, +0.74 a.u., 2.0-fold increase).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 provide validated examples of promoter emergence. The sort-seq data show significant fluorescence increases (Mann-Whitney U tests with very low q-values), and independent plate reader validation confirms the effects. The spacing (17-18 bp) is consistent with canonical promoter architecture. These are well-controlled positive examples.

results.result: Destroying -10 and -35 boxes in non-promoter parents does not create de novo promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3D, where no significant fluorescence increases are associated with motif loss in non-promoter sequences. This negative result is important for ruling out repression by these motifs in non-promoter contexts.

results.result: In promoter parents, losing -10 or -35 boxes exclusively decreases expression (5 and 3 hotspots identified, respectively). For P12-RFP, losing the -35 box decreases fluorescence by -1.57 a.u. and losing the -10 box by -1.41 a.u., with scrambling these motifs reducing fluorescence 62.6-fold and 49.7-fold respectively. No hotspots showed increased expression from motif destruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 demonstrate that -10 and -35 boxes do not repress promoter activity. The statistical tests are highly significant (q-values <10^-60), and experimental validation with scrambled sequences provides strong controls. The absence of expression increases upon motif loss (C58) is a key negative result supporting the conclusion that these motifs do not repress.

results.result: In the 10 promoter parents, 329 new -10 boxes and 332 new -35 boxes were created, but only 4 new -10 boxes and 1 new -35 box increased expression, while 4 new -10 boxes and 6 new -35 boxes decreased expression. These 15 hotspots include 6 homo-motif gains (40%) and 3 hetero-motif gains (20%), occurring at 11 specific positions that partially overlap with preexisting promoter motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 and C125 show that new motifs primarily modulate existing promoters when they overlap with active motifs. The statistical analyses identify significant fluorescence changes, and the categorization into homo- and hetero-gains is well-defined. This demonstrates fine-tuning of promoter strength rather than creation of new promoters.

results.result: Specific examples of promoter modulation include: P12-RFP where a point mutation creates a new -10 box +1 bp from the original while improving the original's PWM score (TACAAT→TAtAAT, +0.78 a.u., 0.3-fold increase), and P22-GFP where mutations change the -35 box into a -10 box, decreasing expression by -0.90 a.u. (13-fold decrease).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide validated examples of promoter modulation through overlapping motif gains. The sort-seq data show significant effects, and plate reader validation confirms the changes. The P22-GFP example (C67-C68) demonstrates that hetero-gains can disrupt promoter function by destroying essential motifs.

results.result: Four of the 15 hotspots (~27%) in promoter parents are located in P20-GFP/RFP, which encodes a bidirectional promoter.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 identifies P20 as having multiple hotspots, consistent with its bidirectional promoter activity. However, the authors note they cannot confidently map this promoter, limiting interpretation of why motif gains increase or decrease expression in this context.

results.result: H-NS represses P22-GFP and P12-RFP in cis, as demonstrated by increased fluorescence in Δhns backgrounds (1.6-fold and 0.5-fold respectively). Mutations destroying H-NS motifs upstream of mapped promoters significantly increase fluorescence (+0.52 a.u. in P22-GFP, +0.53 and +0.51 a.u. in P12-RFP). H-NS also modulates the bidirectionality of P20, increasing GFP expression 2.6-fold while decreasing RFP expression 0.42-fold in Δhns.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C82 and C95-C98 demonstrate H-NS repression through multiple lines of evidence: Δhns knockout experiments, mutational analysis showing fluorescence increases when H-NS motifs are lost, and appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests). The cis-repression is well-supported, though trans-effects cannot be ruled out for P20 (C76, C96).

results.result: In P12-RFP, gaining new -10 or -35 boxes at H-NS binding sites decreases fluorescence (-1.1 and -0.61 a.u. respectively), but this effect is rescued in the Δhns background, demonstrating that the fluorescence decrease results from modulating H-NS binding rather than from gaining the promoter motifs themselves.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C94 provide strong evidence that apparent repression by new motifs is actually due to altered H-NS binding. The rescue experiments (C86, C88, C91, C93) are well-controlled, showing that fluorescence is restored to wild-type levels in Δhns. The non-significant differences between mutant+Δhns and WT (C87, C92) support the interpretation that H-NS binding, not motif gain, causes repression.

results.result: There are 16 additional H-NS motifs surrounding the promoter in P12-RFP that may also regulate P12-RFP.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 identifies additional H-NS motifs computationally but provides no experimental evidence for their regulatory function. This is speculative and would require additional mutagenesis or binding studies to confirm.

results.result: Using a liberal PWM threshold (4.8 bits, 1/4 of standard), 74 UP-like elements were identified that are created or destroyed in the library, with 23 significantly changing fluorescence. However, none increased fluorescence by >0.5 a.u. when gained or decreased by >0.5 a.u. when lost, indicating the UP element plays a negligible role in promoter emergence in this dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 appropriately test the role of UP elements using a very permissive threshold. The lack of substantial effects (C102) despite this liberal approach strongly supports the conclusion that UP elements are not major contributors to promoter emergence in these sequences. The analysis is thorough and the negative result is well-supported.

results.result: Promoter emergence is best predicted by the level of background transcription (pervasive transcription) each non-promoter parent produces, suggesting that sequences producing pervasive transcripts (including promoter islands and antisense strands of existing promoters) may have a proclivity for evolving de novo promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 are supported by the sigmoid relationship between parent fluorescence and Pnew (Figure 1E, C15). The interpretation that background transcription predicts promoter emergence is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism is not directly tested. The evolutionary implications (C105) are appropriately framed as suggestions supported by citations.

results.result: -10 and -35 boxes do not repress promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C126 are supported by the absence of fluorescence increases when motifs are destroyed in promoter parents (C58) and the lack of de novo promoter activity when motifs are destroyed in non-promoters (C51). The H-NS rescue experiments (C83-C94) rule out apparent repression by new motifs. This is a major conclusion challenging prior work.

results.result: Mutations can readily create promoters with a wide dynamic range of activity by creating new motifs that overlap with existing ones, facilitating natural selection's fine-tuning of promoter expression levels within a small, accessible sequence space. This supports the conclusion that true promoters in motif-enriched sequences typically overlap with multiple -10 and -35 boxes.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 synthesize the findings on promoter modulation through overlapping motifs. The data showing both increases and decreases in expression (C60-C62, C65-C68) support the dynamic range claim. The inference about evolutionary accessibility (C108) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The support for prior work (C109, Huerta and Collado-Vides 2003) is appropriate.

results.result: The complexity of promoters is underestimated, as -10 and -35 boxes, extended -10, and UP-elements may be only some components of promoter architecture. Other components may include flanking sequences (important in eukaryotes) and there may be more transcriptional repression in the genome than anticipated.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 are speculative interpretations of the finding that most new motifs don't create promoters. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, these claims lack direct experimental support. The suggestions about flanking sequences (C112) and additional repression (C113) are appropriately cited but remain hypotheses requiring future testing.

results.result: Parent sequences contain on average ~5.32 -10 boxes and ~7.04 -35 boxes, with 18 of the -10 boxes including the TGn motif upstream. 30% of parents have the TGn motif upstream of a -10 box, but only 20% of these parents have promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these descriptive statistics about motif content in parent sequences. One reviewer noted that 'the method of identifying key mutations using mutual information in this paper is well done' and another stated the 'evidence supporting these findings is convincing,' implicitly accepting the motif characterization data.

results.result: The mutagenesis library comprised 245,639 unique daughter sequences with a mean coverage of 93% of possible mutational neighbors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the experimental design, with one stating 'their pooling strategy allows them to characterize expression of many different backgrounds in both directions in extremely high-throughput which is impressive!' The coverage statistics were not questioned.

results.result: 10 out of 50 parent sequences encode promoter activity before mutagenesis, including three on the top strand, seven on the bottom strand, and two bidirectional promoters. The remaining 40 parent sequences are non-promoters with an average fluorescence score of 1.39 a.u.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the classification of parent sequences. One reviewer noted 'the authors have described many examples, including several that are non-obvious, and show convincingly that different sequence backgrounds have different probabilities for gaining or losing promoter activity,' supporting the parent sequence characterization.

results.result: The median Pnew for non-promoter parents is 0.046, with the lowest being 0.002 and the highest 0.41, representing a 205-fold difference. The inflection point of the fitted sigmoid curve is at 1.51 a.u., and the probability that mutations create an active promoter varies more than 200-fold among parent sequences.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accepted the overall finding of variable Pnew, one reviewer stated 'I don't think the fluorescence threshold of 1.5 a.u. for promoter activity is justified, the authors do acknowledge this shortcoming, and even empirically-derived thresholds are still technically arbitrary.' This indicates uncertainty about the threshold used to define promoter activity, which affects Pnew calculations.

results.result: Pnew does not significantly correlate with the number of daughter sequences, GC-content, -10 box counts, or -35 box counts. Six k-mers correlate with Pnew, but these correlations are heavily influenced by an outlier and disappear when it is removed. The probability that mutations create an active promoter is not correlated with the number of promoter motifs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this key finding. One reviewer stated 'the authors express a key finding that the specific landscape of promoter motifs in a sequence affect the likelihood that local mutations create or destroy regulatory elements' and 'show convincingly that different sequence backgrounds have different probabilities for gaining or losing promoter activity.' Another noted 'I particularly enjoyed Figure 1E,' which shows the relationship between Pnew and parent fluorescence.

results.result: A total of 68 hotspots were identified across all 50 parent sequences using mutual information analysis. In promoter parents, hotspots overlap significantly with -10 and -35 boxes compared to scrambled sequences, with similar patterns observed in non-promoter parents. However, there is no significant difference in motif overlap between promoters and non-promoters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the mutual information approach. One stated 'the method of identifying key mutations using mutual information in this paper is well done and should be a standard in future studies for identifying regions of interest.' The hotspot analysis and overlap statistics were not questioned.

results.result: Only ~14% of -10 boxes and ~12% of -35 boxes overlap with hotspots, meaning only ~13% of all -10 and -35 boxes in the parents contribute to promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the overall conclusion that most motifs do not contribute to promoter activity. One reviewer noted 'these findings suggest that we are still underestimating the complexity of promoters,' which aligns with this result.

results.result: Mutations created over 1,500 new -10 and -35 boxes at unique positions in non-promoter parent sequences, with ~22% properly spaced and ~7.3% of new -10 boxes having the TGn motif. However, only ~0.3% of these new boxes actually create new promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported this finding. One stated 'the authors have described many examples, including several that are non-obvious, and show convincingly that different sequence backgrounds have different probabilities for gaining or losing promoter activity.' Another noted 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing.'

results.result: Parent P16-RFP gains promoter activity when mutations create a -10 box 17 bp downstream of a preexisting -35 box, increasing median fluorescence by +1.99 a.u. The majority of new -10 boxes emerge when TAAACA mutates to TAAACt, and experimental validation shows an ~11.2-fold increase in fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the validation experiments. One stated 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing. I appreciate the effort put into validating their results.' The specific example of P16-RFP was not questioned.

results.result: Parent P1-RFP gains promoter activity when mutations create a -35 box 18 bp upstream of a preexisting -10 box, increasing fluorescence by +0.74 a.u. The majority of new -35 boxes emerge when ATGAGT mutates to tTGAGT, and experimental validation shows a ~2.0-fold increase in fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this validated example. One noted 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing,' which applies to this P1-RFP case as well.

results.result: Mutations do not create de novo promoter activity by destroying -10 and -35 boxes in non-promoter parents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding. It is consistent with the overall conclusion that -10 and -35 boxes do not repress promoter activity, which reviewers accepted.

results.result: In promoter parents, 5 hotspots were identified where losing a -10 box decreases expression and 3 where losing a -35 box decreases expression. For P12-RFP, losing these boxes decreases fluorescence by -1.57 a.u. and -1.41 a.u., respectively, with experimental validation showing 62.6-fold and 49.7-fold decreases. No hotspots were found where destroying boxes increases expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings. One stated 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing,' which applies to the P12-RFP validation experiments.

results.result: In promoter parents, 329 new -10 boxes and 332 new -35 boxes are created, but only 4 new -10 boxes and 1 new -35 box further increase expression. Surprisingly, gaining 4 new -10 boxes and 6 new -35 boxes decreases expression. 40% of hotspots show homo-motif gains and 20% show hetero-motif gains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings about motif gains in promoter parents. One noted 'the authors have described many examples, including several that are non-obvious, and show convincingly that different sequence backgrounds have different probabilities for gaining or losing promoter activity.'

results.result: In P12-RFP, a point mutation creates a new -10 box that is +1 bp further from the -35 box and increases the PWM score of the original -10 box, increasing median expression by +0.78 a.u. Experimental validation shows a 0.3-fold increase in fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this validated example. One stated 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing.'

results.result: For parent P22-GFP, mutations can change the -35 box into a -10 box, which decreases expression by -0.90 a.u. Experimental validation shows a 13-fold decrease in fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this validated example. One noted 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing.'

results.result: 4 of the 15 hotspots (~27%) in promoter parents are located in P20-GFP/RFP, which encodes a bidirectional promoter.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding. One noted 'recent work in the field of bacterial gene regulation has raised interest in bidirectional promoter regions' and praised the dataset for enabling study of this phenomenon.

results.result: Six parent sequences were identified as H-NS target candidates. P22-GFP shows the largest fluorescence change in the Δhns background (~1.6-fold increase), and P12-RFP shows a ~0.5-fold increase. For bidirectional promoter P20, GFP expression increases ~2.6-fold while RFP expression decreases ~0.42-fold in the Δhns background, suggesting H-NS modulates directionality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the H-NS analysis. One stated 'I particularly enjoyed Figure 1E, thank you for entertaining my analysis request! Also, the H-NS story is a nice addition showing how transcription factors influence this evolution.' The findings were not questioned.

results.result: Two candidate H-NS motifs were identified in P12-RFP and one in P22-GFP whose destruction is associated with fluorescence increases greater than 0.5 a.u. For P22-GFP, destroying the H-NS motif increases fluorescence by +0.52 a.u. For P12-RFP, destroying H-NS motifs increases fluorescence by +0.53 and +0.51 a.u. These findings demonstrate that H-NS can suppress promoter emergence in certain contexts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the H-NS repression findings. One noted 'the H-NS story is a nice addition showing how transcription factors influence this evolution,' indicating support for these claims.

results.result: H-NS sites in P12-RFP overlap with hotspots where gaining new -35 and -10 boxes decreases fluorescence. Experimental validation shows that constructs with new boxes have lower fluorescence in wild-type backgrounds but higher fluorescence in Δhns backgrounds, with the Δhns background rescuing the fluorescence loss. This demonstrates that expression lowers because mutations modulate H-NS binding, not by gaining the boxes themselves.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these mechanistic findings. One stated 'the validation of mutations on a clean background is well-executed, and the results are convincing,' which applies to these H-NS validation experiments.

results.result: H-NS represses both P22-GFP and P12-RFP in cis and modulates the bidirectionality of P20-GFP/RFP in cis or trans. In P22-GFP, the strongest H-NS motif lies upstream of the promoter. In P12-RFP, the strongest H-NS motifs lie upstream of the -10 and -35 boxes, with 16 additional H-NS motifs surrounding the promoter that may also regulate P12-RFP.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these conclusions about H-NS regulation. One noted 'the H-NS story is a nice addition showing how transcription factors influence this evolution,' supporting these mechanistic interpretations.

results.result: 74 UP-like elements were identified using a less stringent PWM threshold, with 23 significantly changing fluorescence when created or destroyed. However, none increase fluorescence by more than 0.5 a.u. when gained or decrease by more than 0.5 a.u. when lost, suggesting the UP element plays a negligible role in promoter emergence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding. One noted 'the additional analyses that include TGn and UP-element motifs are also well done and highly relevant, as these elements are known to compensate for weaker or absent -35 sequences,' indicating acceptance of the UP element analysis.

results.result: Promoter emergence is best predicted by the level of background transcription each non-promoter parent produces. Sequences that produce pervasive transcripts may have a proclivity for evolving de-novo promoters compared to other sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation. One stated 'I particularly enjoyed Figure 1E,' which shows the relationship between parent fluorescence and Pnew that supports this conclusion.

results.result: -10 and -35 boxes are not likely to repress promoter activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this conclusion. One noted 'the authors express a key finding that the specific landscape of promoter motifs in a sequence affect the likelihood that local mutations create or destroy regulatory elements,' which is consistent with boxes not being repressive.

results.result: Mutations can readily create promoters with a wide dynamic range of activity, facilitating natural selection's fine-tuning of promoter expression levels. True promoters in sequences enriched with promoter motifs typically overlap with multiple -10 and -35 boxes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretations. One stated 'the authors have described many examples, including several that are non-obvious, and show convincingly that different sequence backgrounds have different probabilities for gaining or losing promoter activity,' supporting these conclusions.

results.result: We are still underestimating the complexity of promoters. The -10 and -35 boxes, extended -10, and UP-element may be one of many components underlying promoter architecture. Flanking sequences may play an important role in prokaryotic transcriptional regulation, and there may be much more transcriptional repression in the genome than anticipated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these speculative conclusions. One noted 'this study reveals complex mutational patterns, modeling them could significantly advance our ability to predict bacterial evolutionary trajectories and interpret genomes,' supporting the conclusion about promoter complexity.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C6-C10 regarding baseline promoter activity classification using sort-seq fluorescence assay. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and support the 1.5 a.u. threshold and parent sequence characterization.

Perfect agreement on claims C39-C44, C123-C124 demonstrating that new motif creation is insufficient for promoter emergence. Both evaluations strongly support this central finding with appropriate statistical tests and validation experiments.
Perfect agreement on claim C51 showing no significant fluorescence increases with motif loss in non-promoter sequences. Both accept this negative result as important for ruling out repression.

Perfect agreement on claims C52-C58 demonstrating that -10 and -35 boxes do not repress promoter activity. Both evaluations find the statistical tests highly significant and validation experiments well-controlled.
Perfect agreement on claims C59-C64, C125 showing new motifs primarily modulate existing promoters when overlapping with active motifs. Both accept the categorization and statistical analyses.

Perfect agreement on claim C69 identifying P20 as having multiple hotspots consistent with bidirectional promoter activity. Both evaluations accept this finding and note its relevance to recent work on bidirectional promoters.

Perfect agreement on claims C83-C94 providing strong evidence that apparent repression by new motifs is due to altered H-NS binding. Both evaluations find the rescue experiments well-controlled and convincing.

Perfect agreement on claims C100-C103 regarding UP element analysis. Both evaluations accept the permissive threshold approach and support the conclusion that UP elements are not major contributors to promoter emergence.
Perfect agreement on claims C104-C105 regarding background transcription predicting promoter emergence. Both evaluations accept the sigmoid relationship and find the interpretation reasonable.
Perfect agreement on claims C106, C126 concluding that -10 and -35 boxes do not repress promoter activity. Both evaluations support this major conclusion challenging prior work.

Perfect agreement on claims C107-C109 synthesizing findings on promoter modulation through overlapping motifs. Both evaluations accept the dynamic range claim and evolutionary accessibility inference.

Divergent evaluations on claims C110-C113. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative interpretations lacking direct experimental support. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the speculative conclusions about promoter complexity and evolutionary implications.

Strong agreement on claims C22-C35 using mutual information to identify functionally important regions. Both evaluations praise the method and accept the hotspot analysis. OpenEval additionally covers C36-C38 about functional motif percentage, which peer reviewers address separately in R7.

Partial agreement on claims C13-C21, C121-C122 about simple sequence features not predicting promoter emergence. OpenEval finds all claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers accept most findings (C16-C22, C122) but express UNCERTAINTY about the 1.5 a.u. fluorescence threshold (C13-C15, C121), questioning its justification.

Agreement on claims C11-C12 demonstrating TGn motif alone is insufficient for promoter activity. Both evaluations accept the computational motif analysis. Peer reviewers also cover C2-C3 in this result regarding parent sequence characterization.

Agreement on claims C45-C47 providing validated examples of promoter emergence in P16-RFP. Both evaluations find the sort-seq data and plate reader validation convincing with appropriate statistical tests.
Agreement on claims C48-C50 providing validated examples of promoter emergence in P1-RFP. Both evaluations accept the validation experiments and canonical spacing findings.
Agreement on claims C65-C66 providing validated examples of promoter modulation through overlapping motif gains. Both evaluations find the validation experiments well-executed and convincing.
Agreement on claims C67-C68 demonstrating hetero-gains can disrupt promoter function (P22-GFP example). Both evaluations accept the validation experiments showing motif destruction effects.

Agreement on claims C4-C5 regarding library size and coverage statistics. Both evaluations accept these descriptive statistics. OpenEval additionally covers C1-C3 about library construction details in this result.

Partial overlap on claims C13-C15, C121 regarding simple sequence features and Pnew calculations. OpenEval finds all claims SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY specifically about the 1.5 a.u. fluorescence threshold justification, though accepting the overall finding of variable Pnew.
Agreement on claims C71-C76 demonstrating H-NS repression through knockout experiments. Both evaluations accept the findings and praise the H-NS analysis as a valuable addition.
Agreement on claims C77-C82 demonstrating H-NS repression through mutational analysis. Both evaluations accept the statistical tests and cis-repression findings.
Agreement on claims C2-C3 characterizing parent sequences using PWM methods. Both evaluations accept the motif characterization data. OpenEval additionally covers C1, C4-C5 in this result.
Agreement on claims C95-C98 regarding H-NS regulation mechanisms. Both evaluations accept these conclusions about H-NS influence on promoter evolution.

Divergent evaluations on claim C99 identifying additional H-NS motifs computationally. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of experimental evidence. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting the computational predictions within the broader H-NS story.

Agreement on claims C36-C38 regarding the key finding that only ~13% of motifs are functional. Both evaluations accept this result as challenging assumptions about motif activity and promoter complexity.
